chapters.title: Chapter 2: Behavioral Economics in Everyday Money Decisions

lessons.title: Subscription Traps: Free Trials, Auto-Renewals, and the Endowment Effect

children.text: Back in Chapter 1, Ritika kept paying for three subscriptions she had forgotten she had, because cancelling felt like a hassle. Look closer and "hassle" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. A ₹149 music app, a ₹499 OTT platform, and a ₹99 cloud storage plan she barely opens don't cost much individually, and cancelling any one of them takes at most a few taps. So why do millions of people, Ritika included, let small unwanted subscriptions run for months or years? This lesson closes the chapter with the mechanism that makes cancelling something you don't even want feel like giving something up.

body.text: Once you possess something, even a subscription you signed up for during a free trial and barely use, you start valuing it more than you would if you were deciding whether to buy it fresh today. Cancelling doesn't feel like declining a purchase. It feels like a loss, and loss aversion makes losses hurt more than equivalent gains, which is exactly why so many subscriptions survive on inertia alone.

children.text: The Endowment Effect: Why Giving Something Up Feels Like a Loss

markDefs.definition: The tendency to value something more highly simply because you own or possess it, compared to how you would value the identical thing if you did not yet own it. First described by Richard Thaler in 1980.

children.text: in 1980, and a decade later Thaler, Daniel Kahneman, and Jack Knetsch demonstrated it in a now-famous 1990 experiment. Some participants were given a coffee mug and asked the lowest price they would sell it for. Others were shown the same mug and asked the highest price they would pay to buy one. Owners consistently demanded roughly twice as much to give up the mug as non-owners were willing to pay for it, even though it was, in every practical sense, the exact same mug. Ownership alone had doubled its felt value.

This is loss aversion from Chapter 1, applied specifically to ownership. Selling the mug, or cancelling the subscription, is coded by the brain as a loss from a reference point of "this is mine," not as a neutral decision about whether the thing is worth its price. And losses, prospect theory showed, are felt roughly twice as intensely as equivalent gains, which is precisely the ratio the mug experiment found.
Free Trials: Manufacturing a Feeling of Ownership

A free trial is not really about letting you test a product before paying. It is about letting the endowment effect start working on you before you have paid a rupee. From day one of a free trial, you have full access, your watch history, your saved playlists, your cloud files are already building up inside the service. By the time the trial ends, you are not deciding whether to buy something new. You are deciding whether to give up something that already feels like yours, complete with data and habits attached to it. That reframing alone converts far more trial users into paying subscribers than the product's actual quality would justify on its own.
Auto-Renewal: Removing the Moment You'd Actually Decide

Auto-renewal then locks the endowment effect in place using two tools from earlier in this chapter, working together. Continuing to pay is the default, exactly like the EPF contribution rate nobody revisits in Lesson 1, so the subscription simply persists unless you take deliberate action against it. And the renewal charge itself is decoupled, silently debited from a saved card with no felt moment of paying at all, exactly the mechanism from Lesson 2. Compare the two ends of a subscription's life, and the asymmetry becomes obvious.

columns.label: Starting a subscription
points: One tap or click, often pre-filled payment details
No confirmation screen questioning the decision

columns.label: Cancelling a subscription
points: Often buried several menus deep, sometimes requiring a support chat or phone call
May only take effect at the end of a billing cycle
A retention offer or confirmation screen questioning the decision
Framed around everything you are about to lose

body.text: India's Central Consumer Protection Authority named "subscription traps" directly in its 2023 Dark Patterns guidelines, defined as making cancellation significantly harder than sign-up. The comparison above is not a design accident in most cases. It is the intended outcome of two separate, deliberately asymmetric flows.

body.title: Price Ritika's forgotten subscriptions
body.prompt: Ritika's ₹149 music app, ₹499 OTT platform, and ₹99 cloud storage plan have all been auto-renewing monthly for a full year, mostly unused. In total, how many rupees has this cost her over the year?
body.explanation: (₹149 + ₹499 + ₹99) × 12 months = ₹747 × 12 = ₹8,964. No single monthly charge felt significant enough to notice, which is exactly the point: the endowment effect and decoupling work charge by charge, not on the annual total most people never actually add up.

body.title: The retention offer
body.scenario: Arjun tries to cancel a gym membership he has visited four times in eight months. The cancellation flow shows a screen: "We'd hate to see you go! Here's 50% off your next 3 months." Arjun accepts the offer and keeps the membership, telling himself he'll definitely start going more often now that it's cheaper.
body.prompt: Which concept from this lesson is the retention offer exploiting, and is Arjun's stated reason for accepting likely to hold up?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The retention offer is exploiting the endowment effect directly: framing cancellation as "leaving" something rather than simply declining to keep paying for a gym he rarely uses, at the exact moment ownership feels most at risk.
2. It also layers in loss aversion through the discount itself: turning down 50% off feels like an active loss, separate from the membership question entirely, even though the real decision is whether ₹0 or a discounted fee is better spent on an unused gym.
3. Arjun's stated reason, that a lower price will make him go more often, is not well supported by his actual pattern of four visits in eight months. The price was never the barrier to attendance, so a discount is unlikely to fix it.
4. A cleaner test would have been to ask, independent of any discount screen: "If I did not already have this membership, would I sign up for it today at this price, given how often I actually go?" That question strips out both the endowment effect and the retention offer's loss framing.

body.title: Endowment effect or loss aversion?
body.question: A user is offered ₹200 cashback to switch from their current food delivery app to a new competitor with identical prices and delivery times. They decline, saying they'd rather "stick with what they know." Is this primarily the endowment effect, or general loss aversion?
options: The endowment effect, because they are treating their current app as something they own and are reluctant to give up, even though switching costs them almost nothing
Loss aversion in general, unrelated to ownership, since no physical or financial asset is being given up
Neither, this is simply a rational preference for a familiar interface
Both are equally impossible to distinguish in this example
body.explanation: The user isn't weighing a generic loss against a generic gain, they are specifically overvaluing the app they already use, purely because it is the one they already use. That specific pattern, valuing what you already have more than an identical alternative, is the endowment effect, which is loss aversion applied narrowly to ownership and habitual use rather than loss aversion on its own.

body.title: Name the effect
body.textWithBlank: Valuing something more highly simply because you already own or use it, compared to how you would value the identical thing before owning it, is called the ___ effect.
body.explanation: The endowment effect explains why cancelling a barely used subscription, or giving up a coffee mug you were handed minutes ago, feels like losing something rather than simply declining a purchase.

body.title: Why did the mug experiment matter so much to economists?

children.text: Standard economic theory, built on the Coase theorem, predicted that once a mug was handed out at random, roughly half the recipients should end up trading it to the people who wanted it more, regardless of who started out owning it. Ownership was assumed not to matter to value, only genuine preference should. The 1990 mug experiment found trading volumes far below that prediction, precisely because owners priced their mugs well above what non-owners would pay. It became one of the most widely replicated results in behavioral economics, and a direct empirical challenge to a specific, testable prediction of classical theory, which is part of why it is still taught today.

body.label: The mug experiment's ratio
body.context: Owners demanded roughly twice what non-owners offered for an identical mug, closely matching the loss-aversion ratio from prospect theory.

cards.definition: Valuing something more highly simply because you own or possess it, compared to its value before you owned it. Named by Thaler in 1980.
Kahneman, Knetsch, and Thaler's 1990 study finding mug owners demanded roughly twice what non-owners would pay for an identical mug.
A discount or incentive shown at the moment of cancellation, designed to exploit the endowment effect's loss framing rather than address the actual reason for cancelling.
A dark pattern, formally named in India's 2023 CCPA guidelines, where cancelling a service is made significantly harder than signing up for it.

The classical economic prediction that, absent transaction costs, goods will end up with whoever values them most, regardless of initial ownership. The endowment effect is a direct empirical challenge to this prediction.

points: The endowment effect makes people value something more simply because they already own or use it, and cancelling it register as a loss rather than a neutral decision.
Free trials work by letting ownership feelings build before any payment is due, so the real decision at trial's end is reframed from "buy this" to "give this up."
Auto-renewal locks this in using two mechanisms from earlier in the chapter: continuing is the default, and the charge itself is decoupled from any felt moment of paying.
India's 2023 Dark Patterns guidelines now name subscription traps directly, and the asymmetry between an effortless sign-up and a difficult cancellation is rarely accidental.

Across this chapter, the same handful of mechanisms, defaults, decoupling, present bias, and the endowment effect, keep resurfacing under different names in EMIs, insurance, and now subscriptions, because they are the same few levers on the same few human tendencies.
